The 1904 Olympic marathon might be the strangest race in history.
The winner was poisoned. The first man across the line rode in a car. And one runner stopped for a nap.
Here's how it happened.
St. Louis, August 1904. The Olympics are part of a giant World's Fair.
Thirty-two runners line up for the marathon. It's over thirty degrees, the roads are dirt, and the course is full of steep hills.
Officials and doctors drive ahead of the runners in cars, so the runners spend the whole race choking on dust.
And there's only one place to get water along the entire course.
That's on purpose. The organizer, James Sullivan, wants to see what happens when athletes don't drink.
So what happens?
One American runner, William Garcia, is found collapsed by the road. The dust has torn his stomach lining, and he nearly dies.
Another runner starts vomiting, and quits.
Then there's Andarin Carvajal, a mailman from Cuba.
He raised money to get to St. Louis, lost it all gambling in New Orleans, and had to hitchhike the rest of the way.
He runs in his street clothes, with his trousers cut off at the knee.
Along the way, he gets hungry, and eats some apples from an orchard. They're rotten.
His stomach cramps so badly, he lies down at the side of the road, and takes a nap.
Then he wakes up, keeps running, and still finishes fourth.
Two Tswana men from South Africa, Len Tau and Jan Mashiani, become the first black Africans to compete in the Olympics.
Len Tau gets chased about a mile off course by wild dogs. He still finishes ninth.
Meanwhile, American Fred Lorz gets cramps after nine miles, and gives up.
So he climbs into a car.
He waves at the other runners as he rides past them, for about eleven miles.
Then the car breaks down. So Lorz gets out, and jogs the rest of the way.
He enters the stadium first. The crowd goes wild.
He's photographed with the President's daughter, Alice Roosevelt, and he's just about to get the gold medal.
Then someone shouts that he rode in a car.
Lorz says it was a joke. He's banned for life.
The ban gets lifted, and the next year he wins the Boston Marathon. Without a car.
So who actually won?
Thomas Hicks, an Englishman running for America. He was miles ahead, but he was falling apart.
When he begged for water, his trainers said no, and gave him something else. Strychnine. Rat poison.
Mixed with raw egg whites.
Back then, people thought a tiny dose of strychnine could make you run harder.
A few miles later, Hicks got a second dose. This time, with brandy.
By the end, he was hallucinating. He thought the finish line was still twenty miles away.
His trainers held him up, and practically carried him across the line.
His time, three hours and twenty-eight minutes, is still the slowest winning time in Olympic marathon history.
It took four doctors to get him well enough to leave the stadium. He'd lost eight pounds in one race.
Of thirty-two runners, only fourteen finished.
Some officials wanted to scrap the marathon for good.
Instead, at the next Olympics, the runners got something new. Water.
